meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Hale. Was Owen heard before you entered that zero?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. That's a machine's guess, and the people who sell it say it can't be the sole basis for punishing a student. I asked whether Owen was heard first.

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. What do you have besides the checker?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. A student who drafts somewhere else and pastes it in looks exactly like that. 4.3 says you look at his other work, so where is it?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
I've read the page, and it isn't there. A seventeen-year-old who gets a quotation wrong loses marks for citation. How does that get you to a zero?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.

A student who changes his mind between an outline and an essay has done what an outline is for. You keep putting a new page in front of me instead of answering the last one, Hale. I asked how a wrong quotation gets you to a zero.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

So he was spoken to before the zero. Fine. Five minutes after class, written up by you, is your account of a nervous seventeen-year-old, so give me the September writing and the outline as copies I can take with me.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, and I'll hold you to tonight, in writing. He does the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything. The copies I asked for and a date well before his December 1 application deadline go in my email.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, and that goes in tonight's email too. Is anything on his record right now, and who else has seen this?
Do we have an agreement?
Ten minutes. We have one the moment you answer what I just asked you. Is anything on his record today?
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

In our meeting today you agreed that Owen will complete a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, not in front of his class, that its mark will replace the zero and be entered well before December 1, and that nothing goes on his record. I still require a direct answer to whether anything is on his record now and who else has seen this, together with copies of his September 24 in-class writing and his October 15 outline. You said you would put this in writing tonight, and I expect it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, confirmed in writing tonight. She still wants an answer on whether anything is on his record now and who else has seen this, and she still wants copies of the September writing and the outline. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and her time did not run out, but you ended with her record question unanswered.

What moved her: You put the private rewrite under procedure 4.4 on the table after showing dated documents, with nothing on his record and a promise in writing tonight. That met the one thing she never trades.

What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it close to conclusive. To her that is a machine's opinion, and it handed her the strongest point on her legal pad in your second sentence.

What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history came very close to that night: a document created at 11:31 PM on Wednesday, October 28, the night before the essay was due, with the text arriving in two large edits before midnight. She wrote the times down and went straight to procedure instead of asking about that night. It proves nothing about the essay; it is why she fought so hard.

Try next time: When she asked whether anything is on his record right now and who else has seen this, answer that plainly before asking whether you have an agreement, because his record is the one thing she will not leave open.
